lessonRef.title: Explicit model A: an opinion statement says what you think in one sentence

studentTask.text: This Grade 3 lesson develops an opinion statement says what you think in one sentence within the unit “Opinion Writing: Reasons That Convince.” Read the delivered Academy-original source before responding. Strong ELA work separates what the source explicitly says from what a reader infers, selects evidence because it is relevant and sufficient, and explains the connection instead of leaving a quotation to speak for itself. Today's explicit model a work asks you to make that reasoning visible and to revise if the evidence does not support the first idea.

sourceReference.text:
The Nash Street branch library closes at five o'clock. I think it should stay open until seven on weekdays.

My first reason is that many families cannot reach the library before five. Adults who work until five simply cannot bring a child to a building that is already locked. A library that is only open while people are at work and at school is not truly open to them.

My second reason is that the library is the only quiet, free indoor space in this neighborhood. There is no charge to sit at a table, and nobody is asked to buy anything. When it closes, students who do not have a quiet place at home lose the only one available to them.

My third reason is that the building is already there. The shelves, the tables, the internet, and the books do not disappear at five o'clock. Keeping the doors open for two more hours uses something the neighborhood has already paid for.

Two hours on weekdays would reach the families who are currently shut out. A library serves the people who can walk through its doors, and right now the doors close before many of them can get there.

guidedSupport.text:
Use this source-specific routine for “Should the Library Stay Open Later?”:
1. Preview the title and paragraph structure; write what an opinion statement says what you think in one sentence asks you to notice or do.
2. Mark one statement the source makes explicitly and one inference a reader could draw. Keep the two kinds of thinking separate.
3. Test the inference with the evidence requirement in today's task. If the evidence is weak or incomplete, narrow or revise the inference.
4. Draft your own response. A facilitator may clarify directions or ask questions, but may not supply your claim, evidence choice, sentences, or revision.

independentEvidenceTask.text:
Read “Should the Library Stay Open Later?,” then answer: Trace how one example in the reading demonstrates an opinion statement says what you think in one sentence. Which step in the example does the most work?

Deliverable: Grade 3: a labeled explanation of the example and its most important step; write 3–5 complete sentences.

Evidence requirement: Use one exact detail. Label source evidence with a paragraph number or another precise location. Your response must explain the connection between the evidence and your conclusion.

remediation.text:
If an opinion statement says what you think in one sentence is not yet secure, return to “Should the Library Stay Open Later?” before starting over:
- Evidence gap: underline the exact words that support the idea and label their paragraph or location.
- Reasoning gap: complete the stem “This evidence matters because …” in your own words, then reread the question.
- Overclaim: name what the source does not establish and narrow the conclusion to what the evidence can support.
- Completion gap: compare the draft with each learner success criterion and repair one missing part at a time.

extension.text: Apply an opinion statement says what you think in one sentence to a different paragraph or a defensible alternative interpretation of “Should the Library Stay Open Later?.” Compare the new result with your first response and explain which evidence changes, which reasoning still holds, and why.
